Paradise Lost.note: Blank-verse epic: 10 books (1667) → 12 (1674). Aim: “justify the ways of God to men”. Satan dominates Books I–II; the Fall is Book IX.

MLA Handbook.note: 9th edition (2021). Know the core elements in order: author, title of source, container, other contributors, version, number, publisher, date, location. Three or more authors → “et al.”

Course in General Linguistics.note: Published 1916 after his death, from students’ notes (Bally & Sechehaye). Sign = signifier + signified, arbitrary. Langue/parole, synchronic/diachronic, syntagmatic/paradigmatic.

An Apology for Poetry.note: Same essay, two titles: written c. 1580, printed 1595. Answers Gosson’s School of Abuse (1579). Poet beats philosopher and historian; poetry teaches and delights; nature’s world is “brazen”, the poet’s “golden”.

The Canterbury Tales.note: c. 1387–1400, unfinished. “Nine and twenty” pilgrims set out from the Tabard Inn, Southwark, for Becket’s shrine; host Harry Bailly; the Knight tells the first tale. Mostly heroic couplets.

The Spectator.note: Daily, 1711–12. Mr Spectator’s club, Sir Roger de Coverley. Aim: “to enliven morality with wit”. Addison’s papers on Paradise Lost and on the Pleasures of the Imagination.

Hamlet.note: c. 1600–01 revenge tragedy. Play within the play (The Mousetrap), Yorick’s skull, “To be, or not to be”. Eliot’s “Hamlet and His Problems” (1919) gives the objective correlative.

An Essay of Dramatic Poesy.note: 1668 dialogue on a Thames boat during the 1665 sea battle. Crites (ancients), Eugenius (moderns), Lisideius (French), Neander (English = Dryden). Defends rhyme; praises Shakespeare.

Of Grammatology.note: 1967; English by Gayatri Spivak (1976). Attacks logocentrism and phonocentrism; the supplement (via Rousseau); “there is nothing outside the text”.

Seven Types of Ambiguity.note: 1930, by I. A. Richards’s student. Close reading of verbal ambiguity in seven types, ending with full contradiction that shows a division in the writer’s mind.

King Lear.note: c. 1605–06. Double plot: Lear’s daughters and Gloucester’s sons (Edgar, Edmund). The Fool, the storm on the heath, Cordelia’s “Nothing”. Nahum Tate gave it a happy ending (1681).

Poetics.note: c. 335 BCE. Tragedy imitates an action and brings catharsis through pity and fear. Six parts, plot first. Hamartia, peripeteia, anagnorisis; unity of action.

The Faerie Queene.note: Books I–III 1590, IV–VI 1596 (12 planned). Allegory for Elizabeth (Gloriana); Book I: Redcrosse Knight, Holiness. Spenserian stanza: 9 lines, ababbcbcc, ending in an alexandrine.

Lives of the Poets.note: 1779–81, lives of 52 poets. The Life of Cowley defines the metaphysical poets; the Life of Milton attacks Lycidas.

Biographia Literaria.note: 1817. Chapter XIII: primary and secondary imagination vs fancy. Chapter XIV: “willing suspension of disbelief”. Disagrees with Wordsworth on poetic diction.

The Way of the World.note: 1700 comedy of manners. Mirabell and Millamant’s “proviso scene” (Act IV); Lady Wishfort, Fainall, Mrs Marwood.

The Waste Land.note: 1922, five parts: Burial of the Dead, A Game of Chess, The Fire Sermon, Death by Water, What the Thunder Said. Edited by Pound (“il miglior fabbro”); Tiresias; ends “Shantih shantih shantih”.

Ulysses.note: Paris, 1922 (Shakespeare and Company). One day, 16 June 1904 (“Bloomsday”); Bloom, Stephen Dedalus, Molly’s closing “yes”. 18 episodes mirroring the Odyssey; stream of consciousness.

Utopia.note: 1516, in Latin; English by Ralph Robinson (1551). Raphael Hythloday describes the island; the title puns on “no place” and “good place”.

Culture and Anarchy.note: 1869. Culture = “the best which has been thought and said”; “sweetness and light”; Hellenism vs Hebraism; Barbarians, Philistines, Populace.

An Essay on Criticism.note: 1711, heroic couplets. “A little learning is a dang’rous thing”, “To err is human, to forgive divine”, “Fools rush in where angels fear to tread”.

Look Back in Anger.note: Royal Court, 1956: the “Angry Young Men” and kitchen-sink drama. Jimmy Porter, Alison, Cliff, Helena; the ironing board; the bear-and-squirrel game.

A Literature of Their Own.note: 1977. Women’s writing in three phases: Feminine (1840–80), Feminist (1880–1920), Female (1920 on). She later coined “gynocriticism”.

Culture and Society.note: 1958. Traces the idea of “culture” in British thought, 1780–1950, through keywords like industry, democracy, class, art and culture.

The Advancement of Learning.note: 1605, in English, for James I. Maps human knowledge and lists the “distempers” of learning. Trap: the four Idols are in Novum Organum (1620), not here.

The Tempest.note: c. 1610–11, his last solo play. Prospero, Miranda, Ariel, Caliban; keeps the unities. Central to postcolonial readings; Césaire rewrote it as Une Tempête (1969).

The Pilgrim's Progress.note: 1678 (Part II 1684), a dream allegory begun in Bedford gaol. Christian, Evangelist, the Slough of Despond, Vanity Fair, the Celestial City.

Macbeth.note: c. 1606, the shortest tragedy. Witches, the Porter scene, “Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow”. De Quincey’s essay “On the Knocking at the Gate in Macbeth” (1823).

The Location of Culture.note: 1994. Hybridity, ambivalence, the Third Space, the “unhomely”; mimicry as “almost the same, but not quite”.

Waiting for Godot.note: French 1953, English 1955. Vladimir, Estragon, Pozzo, Lucky, a Boy; opens “Nothing to be done”. Theatre of the Absurd; Mercier: a play where “nothing happens, twice”.

The Well Wrought Urn.note: 1947, New Criticism. “The Language of Paradox” and “the heresy of paraphrase”; readings of Donne’s “The Canonization” and Keats’s Grecian Urn.

A Room of One's Own.note: 1929, from 1928 talks at Newnham and Girton. A woman needs “money and a room of her own” to write; Shakespeare’s imagined sister Judith; the androgynous mind.

Sons and Lovers.note: 1913, Nottinghamshire mining country. Paul Morel torn between his mother Gertrude and Miriam Leivers, then Clara Dawes; an Oedipal novel.

The Wretched of the Earth.note: 1961, preface by Sartre. On the violence of decolonisation, national consciousness and national culture; three phases of the native intellectual.

Practical Criticism.note: 1929, from Cambridge experiments with unsigned poems. Four kinds of meaning: sense, feeling, tone, intention; “stock responses”.

Wide Sargasso Sea.note: 1966 prequel to Jane Eyre: Bertha’s story as Antoinette Cosway, from Jamaica (Coulibri) to Dominica; Rochester narrates Part Two, unnamed.

Mythologies.note: 1957. Everyday “myths” (wrestling, wine, Einstein’s brain, the Paris-Match saluting soldier); myth as a second-order sign system.

Jane Eyre.note: 1847, as “Currer Bell”. Lowood, Thornfield, Bertha in the attic; “Reader, I married him.” Basis of Gilbert & Gubar’s The Madwoman in the Attic and Rhys’s Wide Sargasso Sea.

Gulliver's Travels.note: 1726. Four voyages: Lilliput, Brobdingnag, Laputa (with Balnibarbi, Glubbdubdrib, Luggnagg, Japan), the Houyhnhnms and Yahoos. Big-Endians vs Little-Endians.

Aspects of the Theory of Syntax.note: 1965, the “Standard Theory”. Competence vs performance; deep and surface structure. Comes after Syntactic Structures (1957).

Tess of the d'Urbervilles.note: 1891, subtitled “A Pure Woman”. Alec and Angel Clare; Wessex; ends at Stonehenge and “the President of the Immortals … had ended his sport with Tess”.

Essays.note: 1597 (10), 1612 (38), 1625 (58). Aphoristic. “Of Studies”: “Studies serve for delight, for ornament, and for ability”; “Of Truth”: “What is truth? said jesting Pilate”.

Hayavadana.note: 1971, Kannada. From Thomas Mann’s The Transposed Heads, rooted in the Kathasaritsagara. Devadatta, Kapila, Padmini; a Bhagavata narrator; the horse-headed man.

The Handmaid's Tale.note: 1985 dystopia of Gilead, narrated by Offred; Aunt Lydia; a “Historical Notes” epilogue. Atwood calls it speculative fiction.

The Dialogic Imagination.note: Essays, English 1981 (ed. Holquist). Dialogism, heteroglossia, the chronotope; the open novel vs the closed epic.

Kanthapura.note: 1938. A Gandhian village in Mysore, told by grandmother Achakka; Moorthy. The foreword is on writing in English, “a language that is not one’s own”.

Orientalism.note: 1978. Uses Foucault’s idea of discourse: the “Orient” as the West’s construction. Latent vs manifest Orientalism; Flaubert and Kuchuk Hanem.

Culture and Imperialism.note: 1993. “Contrapuntal” reading of empire in canonical texts: Mansfield Park (Antigua), Kim, Heart of Darkness, Verdi’s Aida.

Lyrical Ballads.note: 1798, anonymous. Opens with the Ancient Mariner, ends with Tintern Abbey. Wordsworth’s Preface added in 1800, enlarged in 1802.

Preface to Lyrical Ballads.note: 1800/1802. Poetry is “the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings … recollected in tranquillity”; “a selection of language really used by men”; the poet as “a man speaking to men”.

Beloved.note: 1987, Pulitzer 1988. Sethe and the haunted house at 124 Bluestone Road; based on Margaret Garner; dedicated to “Sixty Million and more”.

Untouchable.note: 1935, one day in Bakha’s life; preface by E. M. Forster. Three “solutions”: Christianity, Gandhi, and the flush toilet.

The Implied Reader.note: 1972 (English 1974), reader-response theory. The text’s gaps or blanks are filled by the reader; followed by The Act of Reading (1976).

Othello.note: c. 1603–04, from Cinthio. Iago, Desdemona, the handkerchief. Coleridge on Iago’s “motiveless malignity”; Rymer’s attack (1693).

The Postmodern Condition.note: 1979, a report on knowledge for Quebec. Postmodernism as “incredulity toward metanarratives”; language games.

The Deserted Village.note: 1770. Auburn, “loveliest village of the plain”, emptied by enclosure. “Ill fares the land … where wealth accumulates, and men decay.”

Frankenstein.note: 1818 (revised 1831), “The Modern Prometheus”. Born of the 1816 ghost-story contest at Villa Diodati; Walton’s letters frame it; the creature reads Paradise Lost.

The Death of the Author.note: 1967 (Aspen), French 1968. The text is “a tissue of quotations”; the author gives way to the “scriptor”; “the birth of the reader must be at the cost of the death of the Author”.

The Rainbow.note: 1915, seized for obscenity. Three generations of Brangwens ending with Ursula; continued in Women in Love.

Black Skin, White Masks.note: 1952. The psychology of colonised Black people: language, race, the white gaze (“Look, a Negro!”), epidermalisation.

The Tatler.note: 1709–11, three times a week, written as “Isaac Bickerstaff”; Addison joined. Forerunner of The Spectator.

Distinction.note: 1979. Taste marks class: cultural capital, habitus, and the “new cultural intermediaries”.

Great Expectations.note: 1860–61 (All the Year Round). Pip, Magwitch, Miss Havisham, Estella; the ending was softened on Bulwer-Lytton’s advice.

Life of Cowley.note: In Lives of the Poets (1779). Defines the metaphysical poets: “heterogeneous ideas … yoked by violence together”, a kind of discordia concors.

The Country Wife.note: 1675 Restoration comedy. Horner pretends to be impotent; Margery Pinchwife; the notorious “china scene”.

The Study of Poetry.note: 1880, introduction to Ward’s The English Poets. Poetry as a “criticism of life”; the touchstone method; Chaucer lacks “high seriousness”; Dryden and Pope are “classics of our prose”.

How to Do Things with Words.note: 1962, from 1955 Harvard lectures. Speech acts: performatives vs constatives; locutionary, illocutionary, perlocutionary acts.

Marxism and Literature.note: 1977, cultural materialism. Dominant, residual and emergent culture; “structures of feeling”.

Hard Times.note: 1854, dedicated to Carlyle. Coketown, Gradgrind’s “Facts”, Bounderby, Sissy Jupe, Stephen Blackpool. Books: Sowing, Reaping, Garnering.

Vanity Fair.note: 1847–48, “A Novel without a Hero”. Becky Sharp vs Amelia Sedley; Waterloo; the title comes from Bunyan.

Wuthering Heights.note: 1847, as “Ellis Bell”. Narrated by Lockwood and Nelly Dean; Heathcliff and Catherine (“I am Heathcliff”); the Heights vs Thrushcross Grange.

Preface to Shakespeare.note: 1765. Shakespeare is the “poet of nature”, drawing species, not individuals. Defends tragicomedy, rejects the unities of time and place; “a quibble was to him the fatal Cleopatra”.

Modern Painters.note: Five volumes, 1843–60, defending Turner. Volume III (1856) coins the “pathetic fallacy”.

The History of Sexuality.note: Volume 1, 1976. Rejects the “repressive hypothesis”; sex as discourse and power; biopower; scientia sexualis vs ars erotica.

Tradition and the Individual Talent.note: 1919 (The Egoist). The historical sense; impersonality; the poet’s mind as catalyst (platinum). Poetry is “an escape from emotion”.

The Birthday Party.note: 1958. Stanley Webber, his visitors Goldberg and McCann, Meg and Petey; Irving Wardle called it a “comedy of menace”.

Lord of the Flies.note: 1954, an answer to Ballantyne’s The Coral Island. Ralph, Piggy’s glasses, Jack, Simon, the conch. Golding: Nobel 1983.

The Duchess of Malfi.note: c. 1613–14 Jacobean tragedy. Bosola, Ferdinand, the Cardinal, Antonio; “I am Duchess of Malfi still”; “Cover her face; mine eyes dazzle: she died young”.

Bleak House.note: 1852–53 satire on Chancery (Jarndyce and Jarndyce). Opens in fog; two narrators (Esther plus a present-tense voice); Inspector Bucket; Krook’s spontaneous combustion.

Minute on Indian Education.note: 2 February 1835. “A single shelf of a good European library …”; a class “Indian in blood and colour, but English in taste”. Led to the English Education Act, 1835.

Oliver Twist.note: 1837–39 in Bentley’s Miscellany, “The Parish Boy’s Progress”. Attacks the 1834 Poor Law; Fagin, Sikes, Nancy, the Artful Dodger; “Please, sir, I want some more.”

Women in Love.note: 1920 sequel to The Rainbow. Ursula and Gudrun Brangwen with Birkin and Gerald Crich; ends in the Alps.

A Midsummer Night's Dream.note: c. 1595–96. Theseus and Hippolyta’s wedding; Oberon, Titania, Puck; the mechanicals stage Pyramus and Thisbe; Bottom.

A Defence of Poetry.note: Written 1821, printed 1840, answering Peacock’s The Four Ages of Poetry. Ends: “Poets are the unacknowledged legislators of the world.”

The Prelude.note: Versions of 1799, 1805 and 1850 (posthumous, titled by his wife). Addressed to Coleridge; “Growth of a Poet’s Mind”; “spots of time”; the stolen boat.

The Uses of Literacy.note: 1957. Working-class culture vs new mass culture. Hoggart founded Birmingham’s Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies (1964).

Lycidas.note: 1637 pastoral elegy for Edward King. St Peter attacks corrupt clergy; “Fame is the spur”; ends “Tomorrow to fresh woods, and pastures new.” Johnson disliked it.

The Rambler.note: Twice-weekly periodical, 1750–52, 208 essays, nearly all by Johnson.

Prison Notebooks.note: Written 1929–35 in Mussolini’s prison. Hegemony, organic vs traditional intellectuals, the subaltern, war of position.

The Whitsun Weddings.note: 1964. Title poem: a train from Hull to London. Also “Here”, “Mr Bleaney”, “MCMXIV”, “Days” and “An Arundel Tomb” (“What will survive of us is love”). Movement poet.

David Copperfield.note: 1849–50, his most autobiographical novel, in the first person. Micawber, Uriah Heep, Steerforth, Betsey Trotwood, Dora, Agnes.

Doctor Faustus.note: c. 1592; A-text 1604, B-text 1616; from the English Faust Book. Mephistopheles, Good and Evil Angels, the Seven Deadly Sins; “Was this the face that launched a thousand ships”.

Robinson Crusoe.note: 1719, often called the first English novel; inspired by Alexander Selkirk. Friday. Ian Watt reads it as economic individualism.

Midnight's Children.note: 1981 Booker, later Booker of Bookers (1993) and Best of the Booker (2008). Saleem Sinai, born at midnight, 15 August 1947; Padma; swapped with Shiva; magic realism.

The Rape of the Lock.note: Mock-epic: 2 cantos 1712, 5 cantos 1714. Belinda (Arabella Fermor) and the Baron (Lord Petre); sylphs led by Ariel; the game of ombre; the Cave of Spleen.

Measure for Measure.note: c. 1603–04 problem play. The Duke disguised as a friar; Angelo, Isabella, Claudio; Mariana and the bed-trick.

Sexual Politics.note: 1970. Patriarchy as a political system, read through D. H. Lawrence, Henry Miller, Norman Mailer and Jean Genet.

Political Shakespeare.note: 1985, the manifesto of British cultural materialism, set beside American New Historicism (Greenblatt).

The New Criticism.note: 1941. Named the movement; discusses Richards, Empson, Eliot and Winters, and calls for an “ontological critic”.

A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man.note: 1916 (serialised in The Egoist, 1914–15). Stephen Dedalus’s growth as an artist; epiphanies; “silence, exile, and cunning”. Opens with the “moocow”.

Simulacra and Simulation.note: 1981. Hyperreality; the map comes before the territory; Disneyland; four phases of the image.

Keywords.note: 1976. The changing meanings of key words of culture and society, such as culture, class, art, industry and democracy.

Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard.note: 1751, Stoke Poges, heroic quatrains. “Full many a flower is born to blush unseen”; “some mute inglorious Milton”; ends with “The Epitaph”.

Dialectic of Enlightenment.note: 1944/1947, Frankfurt School. Enlightenment turning into myth; the chapter “The Culture Industry: Enlightenment as Mass Deception”.

Middlemarch.note: 1871–72, “A Study of Provincial Life”. Dorothea, Casaubon, Lydgate, Ladislaw. Woolf: one of the few English novels “written for grown-up people”.

Revolution in Poetic Language.note: 1974. The semiotic (including the chora) vs the symbolic; poetic language as a revolutionary force.

Nation and Narration.note: 1990 essay collection on the nation as a narrative; Bhabha’s own essay is “DissemiNation”.

Beowulf.note: Old English epic in one manuscript (Cotton Vitellius A.xv). Grendel, his mother, the dragon; Hrothgar’s hall Heorot. Tolkien’s 1936 lecture; Heaney’s 1999 translation.

Leviathan.note: 1651. Without a sovereign, life is “solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short”; social contract.

Adam Bede.note: 1859, her first novel. Hayslope; Hetty Sorrel’s child-murder trial; Dinah Morris the Methodist preacher; Chapter 17 defends realism.

Voss.note: 1957. A German explorer crossing the Australian interior (based on Leichhardt) and Laura Trevelyan. White: Nobel 1973.

The Metaphysical Poets.note: 1921 review of Grierson’s anthology. The “dissociation of sensibility” set in after the 17th century; “A thought to Donne was an experience”.

Anatomy of Criticism.note: 1957, four essays: modes, symbols, myths, genres. Archetypal myths by season: comedy (spring), romance (summer), tragedy (autumn), irony and satire (winter).

Style.note: 1888 essay, collected in Appreciations (1889). Imaginative prose is “the special art of the modern world”.

Volpone.note: 1606 Venetian satire on greed, a beast fable: Volpone (the fox), Mosca (the fly), Voltore, Corbaccio, Corvino.

A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning.note: Donne’s love poem, printed 1633: the compass conceit and “gold to airy thinness beat”. Also Adrienne Rich’s feminist poem of the same title (1970).

Sailing to Byzantium.note: In The Tower (1928), ottava rima. “That is no country for old men”; the golden bird; “the artifice of eternity”.

Tristram Shandy.note: Nine volumes, 1759–67. Digressions, the black page and marbled page; Uncle Toby; Locke’s association of ideas. Shklovsky called it the most typical novel.
